name: Sample Test (original questions)
source: Original practice questions written for LSAT Trainer. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: City council member: Last year, the neighborhoods that installed new streetlights saw a 20 percent drop in reported burglaries. Therefore, installing new streetlights in every neighborhood of the city will reduce burglaries citywide.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that burglary is the most serious crime in the city
relies on evidence from a source whose impartiality is open to question
draws a conclusion about the cost of streetlights from evidence about their effectiveness
presumes, without providing justification, that the neighborhoods that installed streetlights are representative of the city's other neighborhoods
treats the number of burglaries in a neighborhood as though it were the same as the number of burglars
questions.explanation: The argument generalizes from the neighborhoods that chose streetlights to every neighborhood. If those neighborhoods differ (e.g., they had a lighting problem the others don't), the result may not carry over.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Installing new streetlights in every neighborhood will reduce burglaries citywide.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Neighborhoods that installed new streetlights saw a 20% drop in reported burglaries last year.

breakdown.analysis: The neighborhoods that got streetlights first might be special: maybe they had a dark-street problem the others don't, or they also added patrols. Generalizing from them to every neighborhood assumes they're representative. It's like seeing that glasses improved vision for people who needed glasses and concluding everyone should wear them.

choices.note: The argument doesn't care how serious burglary is compared to other crimes. It only claims burglaries would drop.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Streetlights reduce burglary, so streetlights are the best way to fight crime in our city.

choices.note: No source is identified, and nothing suggests bias in the burglary data.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The streetlight manufacturer's report says burglaries fell, so they must have fallen.

choices.note: The argument never talks about cost. Its conclusion is about burglary, not money.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Streetlights cut burglaries 20%, so they're worth whatever they cost.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument assumes the neighborhoods that installed lights are like all the others. If they differed (say, they were unusually dark before), the result may not carry over.
The argument never mentions burglars. It reasons about burglaries in both premise and conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Burglaries fell 20%, so there are 20% fewer burglars in town.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The Varran wetland's population of marsh frogs has declined sharply over the past decade. A fungal disease that is often fatal to marsh frogs was first detected in the wetland ten years ago. The disease, therefore, is probably responsible for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ecologist's argument depends?
choices: The fungal disease is the only threat to marsh frogs in the wetland.
The fungal disease kills marsh frogs in numbers large enough to affect the size of the wetland's population.
Most marsh frogs that contract the disease die within a year of infection.
No other amphibian species in the wetland has declined over the past decade.
The fungal disease will eventually eliminate the wetland's marsh frog population.
questions.explanation: Negate B: the disease kills too few frogs to affect the population. Then it cannot explain the decline, and the argument collapses. A, C, and E are stronger than the argument needs; D is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fungal disease is probably responsible for the marsh frog decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The frogs declined sharply over a decade; a disease often fatal to them was first detected in the wetland ten years ago.

breakdown.analysis: The timing matches, but a disease that kills a few frogs here and there can't explain a sharp population crash. The argument needs the disease to kill enough frogs to matter. It's like blaming a slow leak for an empty swimming pool; it only works if the leak is big enough. Use the negation test on each answer.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument says 'probably responsible,' not the only threat. Negate it: there are other threats too. The disease could still be the main cause.
choices.negation: The fungal disease is not the only threat to marsh frogs in the wetland.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the disease doesn't kill enough frogs to affect the population. Then it can't explain the decline, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: The fungal disease does not kill marsh frogs in numbers large enough to affect the size of the wetland's population.

choices.note: Too specific. Negate it: most infected frogs don't die within a year (maybe it takes longer). The disease could still drive the decline over ten years.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most marsh frogs that contract the disease die within a year of infection.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Negate it: some other amphibian also declined. Maybe the disease or something else hit it too; that doesn't stop the disease from explaining the frog decline.
choices.negation: At least one other amphibian species in the wetland has declined over the past decade.

choices.note: A prediction the argument doesn't make. Negate it: the disease won't wipe them out entirely. It can still be responsible for the decline so far.
choices.negation: The fungal disease will not eventually eliminate the wetland's marsh frog population.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: Children who eat breakfast every day score higher, on average, on standardized tests than children who do not. So eating breakfast improves children's test performance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nutritionist's argument?
choices: Children who eat breakfast every day also tend to get more sleep than children who do not.
Children who eat breakfast every day tend to come from households with higher incomes than children who do not.
Some children who regularly skip breakfast score well above average on standardized tests.
Standardized tests are administered in the morning in most school districts.
In a study in which randomly selected children were given breakfast at school, their test scores rose relative to those of a similar group of children who were not given breakfast.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from correlation to causation. A randomized study isolates breakfast as the cause. B and A raise alternative causes (weakeners).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating breakfast improves children's test performance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Children who eat breakfast daily score higher on standardized tests, on average, than children who don't.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation. Kids who eat breakfast every day may also sleep more, come from wealthier homes, or have more structured families. Any of those could explain the scores. The best strengthener is an experiment where breakfast is randomly given and scores still rise, which isolates breakfast as the cause.

choices.note: Sleep is an alternative cause of higher scores. This weakens.
Income is another alternative cause. This weakens.
A few exceptions don't affect an average. Irrelevant, or at most a tiny nudge against.
Morning testing might make breakfast seem more plausible as a factor, but it doesn't show breakfast causes higher scores. Too weak to strengthen much.
CORRECT. Randomly selected children given breakfast improved relative to a similar group without it. Randomization removes the alternative causes and directly supports breakfast as the cause.

questions.stimulus: Manager: Since we began allowing employees to work from home two days per week, the number of reports our department completes each month has increased by 15 percent. Clearly, the remote-work policy has made our employees more productive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager's argument?
choices: Other departments that adopted similar policies also saw increases in output.
Employees report greater job satisfaction since the policy began.
When the policy began, the department also hired several new employees, increasing its staff by 20 percent.
A few employees chose to continue working in the office five days per week.
The reports completed since the policy began are about the same length as those completed before it.
questions.explanation: Productivity is output per employee. Staff grew 20% while output grew only 15%, so output per employee actually fell. E rules out an alternative explanation, which strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The remote-work policy has made employees more productive.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the policy began, monthly reports completed have risen 15%.

breakdown.analysis: Productivity means output per person, not total output. If you add more people, total output can rise while each person does less. Quick math: 10 people making 100 reports is 10 each. Add 2 people (20%) and make 115 reports: about 9.6 each. Output went up, productivity went down. Watch for answers that change the denominator.

choices.note: Other departments also improved, which, if anything, fits the idea that remote work helps. Doesn't weaken.
Job satisfaction isn't productivity. Irrelevant, or maybe a slight strengthener.
CORRECT. Staff grew 20% while output grew only 15%, so output per employee actually fell. The policy didn't make employees more productive by this evidence.
A few people staying in the office barely matters. It doesn't explain the 15% rise or undercut it.
Reports being the same length rules out the 'reports got shorter' explanation. That strengthens.

questions.stimulus: All of the paintings in the gallery's east wing were acquired before 1950. Any painting acquired before 1950 has been professionally restored at least once. Therefore, the Ravel landscape has been professionally restored at least once.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The Ravel landscape is in the gallery's east wing.
The Ravel landscape was acquired after 1950.
Every painting that has been professionally restored was acquired before 1950.
Some paintings in the east wing have been restored more than once.
The Ravel landscape has never been displayed outside the gallery.
questions.explanation: Chain: east wing → acquired before 1950 → restored. Placing the Ravel in the east wing completes the chain. C reverses the second conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Ravel landscape has been professionally restored at least once.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: East wing painting → acquired before 1950; acquired before 1950 → restored at least once.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: east wing → acquired before 1950 → restored. The conclusion is about the Ravel, but the premises never mention the Ravel. We just need to plug it into the start of the chain (or the middle). 'The Ravel is in the east wing' does it: east wing → before 1950 → restored.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ravel in the east wing → acquired before 1950 → restored. The chain runs straight through to the conclusion.
Acquired after 1950 means the second rule doesn't apply. That leaves the conclusion unproven, maybe even less likely.
Reverses the second conditional (restored → before 1950). It tells us nothing about whether the Ravel was restored.
About some east wing paintings, not the Ravel. Doesn't connect it to anything.
Display history is irrelevant to restoration.

questions.stimulus: Most of the novelists who won the Harlan Prize in the past twenty years had previously published at least three books. However, none of the novelists who won the prize in that period had previously won any other major literary award.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: No novelist who has won another major literary award has published three or more books.
At least some novelists who had published three or more books won the Harlan Prize without having previously won another major literary award.
The Harlan Prize is not considered a major literary award.
Most novelists who have published at least three books have won the Harlan Prize.
Novelists who win the Harlan Prize rarely win other major literary awards afterward.
questions.explanation: Most winners had 3+ books, and all winners lacked prior awards, so at least some 3+-book novelists won without prior awards. D reverses 'most'; E is about later awards, which the stimulus never mentions.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Most Harlan Prize winners in the past 20 years had published at least three books; 2) none of the winners in that period had previously won another major award.

breakdown.analysis: Combine: most winners had 3+ books, and every winner had no prior major award. So the 3+-book winners are novelists with 3+ books who won the Harlan without a prior award. There's at least one of them (more than half of winners). That's exactly a 'some' statement you can prove.

choices.note: The facts only talk about Harlan winners. Novelists with other awards and 3+ books could be plentiful outside that group.
CORRECT. Most winners had 3+ books, and all winners lacked prior major awards. So at least some 3+-book novelists won the Harlan without a prior major award.
The facts never say whether the Harlan counts as major. 'Any other major award' doesn't settle it.
Reverses the 'most.' Most winners had 3+ books; that says nothing about what share of all 3+-book novelists won.
The facts are about awards won before the Harlan. What winners do afterward is never mentioned.

questions.stimulus: In an experiment, participants who were told that a wine was expensive rated it as tasting better than did participants who tasted the same wine but were told it was inexpensive. Brain imaging showed that regions associated with pleasure were more active in participants who were told the wine was expensive.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Price is the most important factor in consumers' choices of wine.
Expensive wines generally taste better than inexpensive wines.
Most people cannot distinguish between wines on the basis of taste alone.
Participants who were told the wine was expensive misreported their ratings.
Beliefs about a product can affect how pleasurable the experience of consuming it is.
questions.explanation: Same wine, different beliefs, different ratings and different brain activity. E says only 'can', which is all the evidence supports. C and A are too strong; D contradicts the imaging evidence.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Participants told a wine was expensive rated it better than those told the same wine was cheap; 2) pleasure-related brain regions were more active in those told it was expensive.

breakdown.analysis: Same wine, different beliefs about price, different ratings, and different brain activity. So belief about the wine changed the actual experience of pleasure. The supported answer is modest: beliefs CAN affect enjoyment. Anything about what matters most to consumers or whether people can tell wines apart goes beyond the facts.

choices.note: Way too strong. The experiment shows price beliefs affect ratings, not that price is the most important factor in buying wine.
It was the same wine in both groups. The experiment says nothing about whether expensive wines really taste better.
Too broad. The experiment didn't test whether people can distinguish different wines; everyone tasted the same one.
Contradicted by the brain imaging: pleasure regions really were more active, so they weren't just faking their ratings.
CORRECT. Same wine, different beliefs, different pleasure responses. 'Can' is exactly as far as the evidence goes.

questions.stimulus: To reduce accidents, the town of Delford installed a traffic light at its busiest intersection. In the year following the installation, however, the number of accidents at that intersection increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The traffic light was installed at a lower cost than the town had anticipated.
Traffic lights have reduced accidents at busy intersections in many other towns.
Shortly after the light was installed, a new highway exit opened nearby, and traffic through the intersection more than doubled.
Most drivers in Delford approve of the new traffic light.
The number of accidents at Delford's other intersections remained stable during that year.
questions.explanation: If traffic doubled, the accident count can rise even if the light lowered the accident rate. B deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Delford installed a traffic light at its busiest intersection to reduce accidents, but accidents there increased the following year.

breakdown.analysis: The light was supposed to reduce accidents, but the count went up. Classic rate-versus-number puzzle. If far more cars go through the intersection, the total number of accidents can rise even if each car is safer. It's like a bigger crowd at a safer swimming pool: the lifeguard is doing great, but more people means more incidents overall. Look for something that changed the volume.

choices.note: Installation cost has nothing to do with accident numbers.
Deepens the puzzle. If lights work elsewhere, why not here? It doesn't explain the increase.
CORRECT. Traffic more than doubled because of a new highway exit. The light may well have lowered the accident rate per car, while the total count still rose because so many more cars came through.
Driver approval doesn't explain why accidents went up.
Other intersections staying stable means there wasn't a town-wide spike. That rules out one explanation and leaves the puzzle intact.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The new museum's design has been widely praised for its bold use of glass. Yet a building whose primary purpose is to protect fragile artworks should not admit so much sunlight, which fades pigments. The architects, therefore, failed at the most important part of their task, however striking the result may be.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the critic's argument?
choices: A building that protects fragile artworks should not admit much sunlight.
The museum's design has been widely praised for its bold use of glass.
Sunlight fades the pigments of fragile artworks.
The architects failed at the most important part of their task.
The new museum's design is visually striking.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' marks the conclusion. A is a premise that supports it, and B is background that the critic argues against.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The architects failed at the most important part of their task.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A building meant to protect fragile artworks shouldn't admit much sunlight, which fades pigments; the museum uses lots of glass.

breakdown.analysis: 'Therefore' flags the conclusion, and here it really is the main one. The critic concedes the design is praised and striking, then argues it fails the museum's core job. The sunlight point is the reason. Ask 'why do you think they failed?' Answer: because the building lets in sunlight that fades art. That's premise → conclusion.

choices.note: A premise. It's the reason the critic gives for saying the architects failed.
Background the critic is pushing back against with 'Yet.'
Part of the supporting premise (sunlight fades pigments). Supports the conclusion; isn't it.
CORRECT. Marked by 'therefore,' supported by the sunlight point, and it's the critic's ultimate judgment of the design.
A concession ('however striking the result may be'). The critic grants it, then argues past it.

questions.stimulus:
Alicia: Public libraries should eliminate late fees. Such fees deter many low-income patrons from borrowing books at all.

Benjamin: But without late fees, patrons would have little reason to return books promptly, and other patrons would wait longer for popular titles.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Alicia and Benjamin disagree over whether
choices: public libraries should eliminate late fees
late fees deter low-income patrons from borrowing books
popular titles are in high demand at public libraries
patrons would return books promptly in the absence of late fees
public libraries depend on late fees for a significant part of their revenue
questions.explanation: Alicia endorses eliminating fees; Benjamin's 'But' objects to it. Benjamin never addresses B, and Alicia never addresses D, so neither is a point of disagreement.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Alicia: Libraries should eliminate late fees because they deter low-income patrons from borrowing.; Benjamin: Without late fees, patrons wouldn't return books promptly and others would wait longer for popular titles.

breakdown.analysis: Alicia says eliminate fees. Benjamin's 'But' raises a reason not to, so he disagrees with eliminating them. Note that each speaker argues from a different consideration, and neither engages the other's fact. Lesson: to disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no; the shared issue here is the policy itself.

choices.note: CORRECT. Alicia: yes, eliminate late fees. Benjamin: no, because returns would slow. Clean disagreement.
Alicia says yes. Benjamin never addresses whether fees deter low-income patrons. No view from him.
Benjamin implies it, but Alicia says nothing about demand for popular titles.
Benjamin says patrons wouldn't return books promptly; Alicia never addresses that. No disagreement on record.
Neither speaker mentions library revenue.

passages.title: Dendrochronology and panel paintings
passages.text:
For centuries, art historians attributed and dated Northern European panel paintings chiefly by stylistic analysis—comparing brushwork, composition, and iconography with those of securely documented works. Such judgments, however expert, are inherently contestable, and disputes over whether a panel was painted by a master or by a later imitator could persist for generations. Over the past several decades, dendrochronology, the dating of wood by the pattern of its annual growth rings, has offered a means of anchoring these debates in physical evidence.

Many such paintings were executed on oak panels, and because the width of an oak's annual rings varies with climatic conditions, a sequence of rings from a panel can be matched against regional master chronologies compiled from timbers of known date. When the match is secure, the analyst can identify the year in which the outermost surviving ring grew. Yet that year is not the date of the painting. Panel makers trimmed away the sapwood—the outer, softer rings—and the wood was typically seasoned for some years before use. Analysts therefore estimate an earliest plausible date of creation by adding a statistically derived allowance for missing sapwood and a minimum seasoning period.

The resulting date establishes when a painting could first have been made, not when it was made. Dendrochronology thus excels at exclusion. A panel whose wood was felled decades after a master's death cannot be that master's work, whatever its stylistic merits. But a panel whose dating is consistent with an attribution does not thereby confirm it, since imitators active in the same period would have drawn on the same timber supplies. The technique, in short, does not replace connoisseurship; it disciplines it, narrowing the range of hypotheses that stylistic analysis must adjudicate.
passages.subject: humanities

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Dendrochronology has rendered stylistic analysis obsolete as a method of attributing panel paintings.
Dendrochronology provides physical evidence that can rule out some attributions of panel paintings, although it cannot by itself confirm them.
Because panel makers removed sapwood, dendrochronological dates for panel paintings are unreliable.
Disputes over the attribution of Northern European panel paintings have persisted because of the limitations of stylistic analysis.
Regional master chronologies allow analysts to determine the exact year in which a panel painting was created.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the thesis: the technique excels at exclusion but does not replace connoisseurship. A contradicts the final sentence, and E contradicts paragraph two.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement that sums up the passage as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph, especially the final sentence; check against paragraph one's setup.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph one: stylistic analysis is contestable; dendrochronology adds physical evidence. Paragraph two: how it works and why the ring date isn't the painting date. Paragraph three: it tells you the earliest possible date, so it's great at ruling attributions out but can't confirm them; it disciplines connoisseurship rather than replacing it. The main point has to capture both the value (exclusion) and the limit (can't confirm).

choices.note: Contradicts the final sentence: dendrochronology 'does not replace connoisseurship.'
CORRECT. Physical evidence that rules out some attributions but can't confirm them on its own. That's the thesis of the last paragraph and the payoff of the whole passage.
Too negative. The sapwood issue is handled with a statistical allowance; the author doesn't call the dates unreliable.
True according to paragraph one, but it's background. It leaves out dendrochronology entirely, which is what the passage is about.
Contradicts paragraph two: the ring date isn't the painting date, and analysts only estimate an earliest plausible date.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the allowance that analysts add to the date of the outermost surviving ring reflects which one of the following?
choices: rings removed when the sapwood was trimmed, together with the time the wood was seasoned
variations in climatic conditions across different regions
the time a painter typically required to complete a panel painting
errors that occur in compiling regional master chronologies
the period during which imitators of a master were active
questions.explanation: Paragraph two: the allowance covers the missing sapwood and a minimum seasoning period.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the added allowance accounts for, as the passage states.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph two, final two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Detail question: find the line. Paragraph two says analysts add 'a statistically derived allowance for missing sapwood and a minimum seasoning period.' Those two things, missing rings and seasoning time, are the answer. Lesson: on detail questions, match the text, don't reason past it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Missing sapwood rings plus the seasoning period: almost word-for-word paragraph two.
Climate variation is why ring widths differ and can be matched to chronologies. It's not what the allowance covers.
Painting time isn't mentioned. The allowance is for the wood, not the painter's work.
The passage never discusses errors in master chronologies.
Imitators come up in paragraph three as a reason consistency doesn't confirm attribution. They have nothing to do with the allowance.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage about a panel painting whose dendrochronological dating is consistent with its attribution to a particular master?
choices: It was painted by that master.
It was painted before that master's death.
It could nonetheless have been painted by an imitator of that master.
Its stylistic features resemble those of the master's documented works.
Its wood was seasoned for longer than was typical.
questions.explanation: A consistent date does not confirm the attribution because imitators used the same timber, so the panel could still be an imitator's work. B overstates what an earliest-possible date shows.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out what follows about a painting whose ring dating is consistent with its attribution to a master.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph three, the 'But a panel whose dating is consistent...' sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The passage says consistency 'does not thereby confirm' the attribution, because imitators of the same period used the same timber. So the painting could still be an imitator's. Also remember that dendrochronology only gives the earliest possible date, so consistency doesn't even prove the painting was made in the master's lifetime.

choices.note: Exactly what the passage says you can't conclude: consistency doesn't confirm the attribution.
Overstates it. Ring dating only gives an earliest possible date. A panel could be cut from old enough wood yet be painted after the master died.
CORRECT. Imitators of the same period used the same timber, so a consistent date leaves open that an imitator painted it.
Nothing about dendrochronology tells you about the painting's style. A consistent date says nothing on brushwork or composition.
Seasoning length isn't implied. The passage only says analysts add a minimum seasoning period.

questions.stem: The author mentions imitators active in the same period primarily in order to
choices: show that dendrochronology can identify the work of imitators
suggest that most disputed panel paintings were in fact painted by imitators
illustrate the expertise that stylistic analysis requires
argue that timber suitable for panels was scarce during the period
explain why a dendrochronological date consistent with an attribution does not confirm that attribution
questions.explanation: The reference is the 'since' clause supporting the claim that consistency does not confirm an attribution.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up imitators active in the same period.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph three, the 'since imitators...' clause.

breakdown.analysis: The imitators are in a 'since' clause, which means they're a reason. The claim they support: a date consistent with an attribution doesn't confirm it. Because imitators drew on the same timber, wood dates can't tell a master from a contemporary copycat. Lesson: function questions are about why something is there; find what it's supporting.

choices.note: Opposite. The point is that dendrochronology can't distinguish imitators who used the same timber.
Too strong. The author just says imitators could have painted such panels, not that most disputed panels are theirs.
The imitators aren't used to show what stylistic analysis requires. They explain a limit of dendrochronology.
The passage says imitators used the same timber supplies, not that timber was scarce.
CORRECT. The 'since' clause explains why a consistent date doesn't confirm an attribution: imitators of the same era had the same wood.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the use of dendrochronology in attributing panel paintings is best described as
choices: indifference to its methodological details
skepticism that it adds anything to stylistic analysis
enthusiasm for its ability to settle attribution disputes conclusively
appreciation of its value, tempered by recognition of its limits
disapproval of its growing use by art historians
questions.explanation: 'Excels at exclusion' and 'disciplines' connoisseurship are positive, while 'does not thereby confirm it' marks a limit.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about using dendrochronology to attribute panel paintings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph three: 'excels at exclusion,' 'does not thereby confirm,' and 'disciplines it.'

breakdown.analysis: Look at the tone words. 'Excels at exclusion' and 'disciplines' connoisseurship are positive. 'Does not thereby confirm' and 'does not replace' are limits. So: positive, with qualifications. Lesson: on attitude questions, the right answer usually matches the mix of praise and caution, not one extreme.

choices.note: The author explains the method in careful detail (sapwood, seasoning), which is the opposite of indifference.
Too negative. The author says it 'excels at exclusion' and anchors debates in physical evidence.
Too positive. The author explicitly says it can't confirm attributions, so it doesn't settle disputes conclusively.
CORRECT. Real appreciation ('excels,' 'disciplines') balanced by clear limits ('does not thereby confirm,' 'does not replace').
No sign of disapproval. The author values the technique.
